talk.title: An AI Manifesto
talk.thesis: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
talk.speaker: Brad Baker

slides.title: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
slides.kicker: For the one in a thousand
slides.notes: This talk is for the one in a thousand: the people who build with AI, not the people who were issued a seat. You can see something your leadership can't see yet. In the next twenty-five minutes I want to give you the facts and the sentences to take upstairs, so that you come back with capacity instead of a cap. At the end we'll vote, and then we'll take questions.

slides.title: “My company spent my entire 2026 budget in Q1. Can you make this more efficient?”
slides.cite: A client complaint Sam Altman quoted on stage, June 2026. He called token costs “a huge issue” that “never came up” six months earlier.
slides.notes: This is a customer complaint that the vendor's own CEO repeated on stage in June. Six months earlier nobody was asking this question, and now everyone is. The reason that budget ran out in the first quarter is probably sitting in this room. Raise your hand if you've been asked to be more efficient with tokens this year. [pause] Keep it up if the answer from upstairs was a cap. You're the people I'm talking to. Altman's answer is efficiency, and mine is ownership.

slides.title: You're the one in a thousand, which is why the people who sign can't see what you see.

stats.l: people actually building their own agents on a harness: you
you use more tokens than everyone else on the floor combined
until the people next to you are doing it too, on the same meter

slides.source: 1-in-1,000: Brad's field observation of people building their own agents. Spread illustrative.
slides.notes: Picture a floor of a thousand people in your company. Two of them are building agents on a harness, and they use more tokens than the other nine hundred and ninety-eight together. That's you. Surveys will tell your leadership that forty percent of large organizations are scaling agents, but that counts deployments, not builders. Builders are closer to one in a thousand. [advance] Three months later the people around you have started doing the same thing, one demo and one team at a time, and every red stack is on the meter. Your CFO is about to see that curve, and the only tool they have is a cap. The point of this talk is to get to them first with a better option.

slides.title: Your ask upstairs is owned capacity for the people who use the most, not more seats.

cols.v: Demand grows faster than prices fall, so the bill spikes in the quarters you're most productive.
If they cap you, the work moves to tools the contract doesn't cover.
Three levels of capacity you own, and one metered gate to the frontier.

lead.v: Three sentences, two numbers and one ask. You'll leave with all of them.

slides.notes: I'll give you the answer first so you can check my reasoning as we go. The ask you take upstairs is to fund owned capacity for the people who use the most, which is you, instead of buying more seats and capping them. Three things get you there. The meter: demand is growing faster than prices are falling, and that turns into a finance problem. The leak: when you're capped, the work doesn't stop, it moves somewhere nobody can see. The ladder: the setup that fixes both. After that I'll give you one sentence each for your CFO, your CIO and your CEO, and the two numbers that turn a conversation into a purchase order.

slides.title: Token use grew a millionfold while the price fell sixteenfold, so the bill went up.

stats.l: frontier list price per million tokens ($60 → $3.85)

slides.source: Altman on stage, June 2026 (volume); 2020 API launch pricing and Artificial Analysis (price); log-interpolated. $1.3M month: Peter Steinberger's published bill (Tom's Hardware).
slides.notes: This is the first chart to show upstairs. The needle shows tokens per month on a log scale, with one big tick for every factor of ten, from 2019 to 2026. [advance] Usage went up a millionfold. Over the same period the price per million tokens for the best model only fell from sixty dollars to three eighty-five. Leadership keeps hearing that tokens are getting cheaper, and older models are. But the best model stays in roughly the same price range, and usage is growing much faster than prices fall, so the monthly bill went up sixty-four thousand times. At the extreme, one three-person team ran about a hundred coding agents and spent one point three million dollars in a single month. Before your meeting, type your own monthly usage into the box. That number is a good way to open.

slides.title: Flat AI plans tend to end the same way: people get hooked, then they get metered.

example.l: users in 45 days at one large agency, then rationing, because small jobs by hundreds of thousands of people “get expensive real, real fast.”

slides.source: Usage-limit changes, 2026; AI Weekly, Aug 2026 (the agency rollout).
slides.notes: You've seen this as a consumer. A flat plan gets you using the product. Then come five-hour session limits, then weekly limits, then pay-as-you-go charges for anything over. The enterprise version follows the same path with bigger numbers: one large agency went from zero to nineteen thousand users in forty-five days and then had to ration them. Last year AI was a subscription anyone could forecast. This year it's a meter tied to how hard you work, and it spikes in the quarters when you're doing your best work. A CFO can plan around a large number, but not one that grows faster than the budget.

slides.title: The median business spends $137 a person a year on AI, and the leaders spend half a salary.

stats.l: the median business, per employee per year
the top 1% of businesses, growing about 14% a month
Jensen Huang's bar for a $500K engineer: half the salary

slides.source: Ramp AI Index, June 2026 (70,000+ US businesses, annualized); Huang on the record (Tom's Hardware).
slides.notes: So what is a reasonable amount to spend? There are finally benchmarks, and the spread is wide. The median business spends a hundred and thirty-seven dollars per person a year. [advance] The top one percent spend eighty-nine thousand, and that number is growing about fourteen percent a month. [advance] Jensen Huang has said on the record that if a five-hundred-thousand-dollar engineer isn't using two hundred and fifty thousand dollars in tokens, he'd be deeply alarmed. That's half the salary. When you go upstairs, you don't need to defend a big number. Show them where the leaders sit on this scale, and where your company is.

slides.title: Models could do 94% of the tasks in computing jobs, but at work they do about a third.
slides.source: Massenkoff & McCrory, “Labor market impacts of AI,” Anthropic, 5 March 2026.
slides.notes: Spending is one way to see the gap, and work is another. In March, Anthropic published two numbers for each occupation: the share of tasks a model could do, and the share it is actually seen doing at work. For computer and math jobs the first number is ninety-four percent. [advance] The second is thirty-three. [advance] The sixty-one points in between aren't about what the models can do. The loom shows what's holding them back: a clamp, a coin box and a padlock, which stand for permission, plumbing and the meter. You know which of those three is stopping you. Name it when you go upstairs, because it's one of the easiest things for leadership to fund.

slides.title: When they cap you, the work moves to personal accounts, and the contract doesn't cover those.

stats.l: of office workers used AI tools they believed weren't allowed
of them shared work information through those tools
retention on consumer plans when the training setting is on

slides.source: PagerDuty, June 2026 (n = 1,250 office professionals, companies ≥ $500M); Anthropic consumer and commercial terms (Aug 2025), with equivalent terms at every major lab.
slides.notes: The front door is the enterprise contract. It's metered, and your data isn't used for training. [advance] Now suppose they cap it. The work doesn't stop, it backs up. [advance] And some of it goes out the side door, on a personal account. Sixty-six percent of office workers say they've used AI tools they believed weren't allowed, and eighty-eight percent of those shared work information through them. The contract only protects the front door. Enterprise, API and commercial traffic is excluded from training at every major lab, but on consumer plans training is a setting the user controls, with five years of retention if it's on. What leaks that way isn't a database. It's how your company works: which tools, which decisions, and which features you're building next. So the argument for upstairs is that a cap doesn't save money. It moves the work to a place nobody can see.

slides.title: The labs ship new products where their usage is densest: images, code, security, finance and legal.
slides.source: Public product launches, in order; Anthropic Economic Index (30+ categories); Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Oct 2026 (46 vs 58). Heights illustrative; the causal reading is Brad's.
slides.notes: The labs are open about this part. Anthropic publishes an Economic Index, built by sorting millions of conversations into more than thirty categories of work. That's this table. [advance] Image generation. [advance] Software. [advance] Security. [advance] Finance. [advance] Legal. Each of these launches landed where the usage map was densest. I'm not suggesting any lab took a feature from a particular customer. This is aggregate data, using their own published method. The two glass planes are today's scores: the best open-weight model at 46, which you can run on your own hardware without a cap, and the frontier at 58, which is metered. Most of the map sits under the lower plane. [advance] The dashed cell is the question for your leadership: is our area next?

slides.title: Capping tokens starts an eight-step loop, and owned capacity breaks it at step three.
slides.source: PagerDuty, June 2026; AI Weekly, Aug 2026; Anthropic consumer terms, Aug 2025; Anthropic Economic Index.
slides.notes: Put those pieces together and you get a loop, and each step is already happening somewhere. Step one: usage grows quickly, and that's you. [advance] Two: the meter arrives. [advance] Three: they cap you. [advance] Four: people move to personal accounts. [advance] Five: consumer accounts can feed training. [advance] Six: your company's intent becomes part of a lab's roadmap. [advance] Seven: a new product covers the routine eighty percent of your work. [advance] Step eight is the only one your leadership controls. They can't set the labs' prices or decide what a consumer account trains on, but they can decide whether to cap you. Owned capacity without a cap stops the loop at step three, so steps four through seven never happen. That's the whole pitch in one picture.

slides.title: The best open model now beats last spring's frontier at a twentieth of the price.

models.name: Muse Spark Open (Meta)
models.tag: best US open weights · Muse licence

slides.line: Run open weights without a cap on capacity you own, and send only the hard problems to the 58.
slides.source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2 and model pages, read 18 Oct 2026. Blended $/M at 7:2:1 cache-hit:input:output; output speed on the first-party API.
slides.notes: These are today's scores from Artificial Analysis, read on October eighteenth. The frontier, Opus 5.5, scores fifty-eight at about three dollars per million tokens. The best open-weight model in the world, Xiaomi's MiMo, scores forty-six for eighteen cents. Opus 4.8, the frontier in May, scores forty-two at three eighty-five. So an open model you can download today beats the frontier of five months ago at a twentieth of the price. If you need an American model, Meta's Muse Spark Open scores thirty-nine at seventy-eight cents and a hundred and thirty tokens a second. Either way the approach is the same: run routine work on open weights you own, without a cap, and send a problem to the fifty-eight only when it needs it. One caveat: most benchmarks are gamed, so test on your own work before you buy.

slides.title: Own three levels and rent one gate: routine work stays inside, and hard problems go out.

stats.l: open weights on the rungs you own: $0.18 per million tokens, no cap
the frontier, through one gate: $2.94 per million, metered
sensitive context removed on the way out

slides.source: Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v4.3.2, Oct 2026. Token mix illustrative.
slides.notes: This is what you're asking for: three levels of capacity inside the fence. [advance] The first is your own machine, refreshed now with NPU laptops and workstations. [advance] The second is a shared inference box for your team. [advance] The third is the core, the rack-scale build, which comes later and is paid for by the growth you create. [advance] Then there's one gate, which is the only way out. Work that needs the frontier goes through it, it's metered, and sensitive context is removed on the way out. [advance] So two rules apply. Volume on the levels you own has no cap, because you own the capacity. Use of the frontier has to be justified, because that's where the cost and the leak are. Nobody has to pick a model by hand; a router does that.

slides.title: Above 5.3 hours a day, owning the hardware costs less than renting it, and you work about twelve.
slides.source: Lenovo 2026 TCO (vendor study): 5-year life, zero residual, 12% maintenance, $0.12/kWh; ~5.2-month break-even. Frontier and wrapped rates are Brad's reads.
slides.notes: Now the money. Take one item, a million tokens from the same open model, and buy it four ways. On a cloud GPU it costs ninety-seven cents. Through a frontier API at a typical coding mix it's about twelve dollars. A wrapped enterprise LLM service charges up to forty-five. With capacity you own, the price depends on how much you use it. [advance] At three hours a day it's a dollar seventy-one. [advance] At five point three hours a day it matches the cloud, which is about a five-month break-even. [advance] At twelve hours a day, which is closer to how you work, it's forty-three cents. The difference comes down to utilization. You aren't asking them to buy hardware for everyone, only for the people who will keep it busy.

slides.title: When you write the RFP, four parts are drafted inside and two go out with the budget removed.
slides.notes: Many of you write the RFPs your company uses to buy services and software, so let's use one as the example. It's Tuesday, and you're drafting an RFP. [advance] The router splits the work. Requirements, evaluation criteria, security terms and the schedule all come from documents you already have, so agents on your own machines draft them and nothing leaves. Two parts need outside information: market research on who can do the work, and current pricing. [advance] Those two go out through the gate. Before they do, the RFP number, the budget and the evaluation plan are removed, and the request is logged. Your budget and the way you'll score vendors are exactly what a vendor would most like to see. [advance] The outside model only sees a general capability question. The answers come back in, and you make the decisions. Build this for your next RFP and show it to your leadership. It's also how you'll write the RFP for the capacity itself.

slides.title: Your job upstairs is to give each office one sentence it can agree to.
slides.source: The manifesto's three drivers (pricing, security, operations) translated for each office.
slides.notes: This is the part you'll use most. Your leadership doesn't need this whole talk. Each office needs one sentence it can agree to. [advance] For the CFO: a cap ends up costing more than owning capacity. Their concern isn't the size of the number, it's that nobody can predict it. Owned capacity is a number they can predict. [advance] For the CIO: apply the IT rules you already have to models. That means a curated model repository, a gateway on every device, and retrieval that follows your existing access controls. [advance] For the CEO: our decision-making data is either our asset or someone else's training data. [advance] Three offices, three sentences. Make sure each office gets its own.

slides.title: Ask for it in stages: your machine now, the team's box next and the core once it's proven.

steps.v: An emergency refresh for the heaviest users: secured machines with no cap.
A shared workgroup box that everyone else can use.
The core, paid for by the growth you create.
The frontier through one metered gate, for the hard problems.

slides.source: AI-capable PCs pass half of shipments in 2026 (Counterpoint). Power takes the longest to arrange, so plan it now.
slides.notes: Don't ask for a data center. You'll lose that argument. Nobody approves a ten-megawatt facility for usage that doesn't exist yet. Plan it around the people who use it. Now: an emergency refresh for the heaviest users, without waiting for the normal cycle. Next: a shared workgroup box that everyone else can use. The core gets built once you've proven the demand, paid for by the growth you create. The frontier stays available through one gate, metered, for the hard problems. Prices are rising, hardware is hard to get, and power takes the longest to arrange, so this needs to be planned like a capital project rather than filed as an IT ticket.

slides.title: The companies doing this well run agents on a defined workflow, with a person approving key steps.
head: What they did
What it shows
rows: Agents for 90,000 employees; each picks its model; 80–90% of SEC-filing first drafts; mostly on its own hardware.
It works at scale, on their own hardware.
12 agents per enterprise, and half of them operate with no oversight.
Ungoverned agents are the new shadow IT.
11% of planned agent projects reached production; an all-agent company hit 24% task success.
Open-ended loops fail; defined workflows with human approval work.
slides.source: Fortune, Jul 2026; Salesforce 2026 Connectivity Benchmark; Futurum 1H 2026; CMU TheAgentCompany.
slides.notes: If someone upstairs says this is theoretical, point to Cisco. This year it put agents in front of ninety thousand employees, with each agent choosing its own model. AI now writes eighty to ninety percent of the first drafts of their SEC filing narratives, and it runs mostly on their own hardware. Meanwhile the average enterprise runs twelve agents and half of them report to nobody, which helps explain why only eleven percent of planned agent projects reach production. The difference is a defined workflow with a person approving the key steps. Your company's decision-making data is the most valuable thing it will build, so don't run it on someone else's meter.

slides.title: By 2029 every organization will have chosen, by acting or by waiting, so vote for where yours is today.

options.v: Remove the cap for the heaviest users on capacity you own, build the ladder, and put a gateway on every device.
Sign the renewal, cap the heavy users, and rely on the contract to cover traffic it never sees.

slides.notes: So this is the choice. By 2029 the capacity shortage, the renewals and the new products will all have arrived, and the decision you can still make is the one made now. Scan the code and vote for where your organization actually is today, not where you'd like it to be. [wait 30 to 45 seconds, then read the tally] That split is a good picture of the market. If you voted for renting, you now know why you were invited to this talk. (Fallback: show of hands; press 1 for own, 2 for rent.)

slides.title: Renting stays flat for two years and then climbs steeply, while owning keeps paying off.
rented: The renewal comes priced per user, in tiers. It won't be a dollar.
The heaviest users hit the caps within a quarter, and personal accounts take the rest.
By year four a new product reaches your industry, and the routine 80% ships as someone else's feature.
Your best builders leave, and some of them build the product aimed at you.
owned: The full setup is standard: device, workgroup, core and a gated frontier.
Agents have a registry, kill switches and a person approving key steps.
Business data runs on your own hardware and never leaves.
Small teams move faster than large ones, and the team that builds this is the one others copy.
slides.notes: These are the two paths. If you keep renting, the renewal is priced per user, in tiers. The heaviest users hit the caps within a quarter. Spending stays flat for a while and then climbs steeply, and the caps don't stop that; they move the work to tools the contract doesn't cover. By year four a new product reaches your industry. If you own the capacity, the setup becomes standard, agents have real controls, and your business data keeps getting more valuable on your own hardware. This is a moment when small, fast teams can beat much larger ones.

slides.title: On Monday, build the map, log your hours and book three meetings.

roles.v: Every system with an AI feature, who pays for its tokens, which model it uses and what fails when that model is down. One page.
How many hours a day you keep a machine busy, for two weeks. Above 5.3 a day, owning the hardware pays off.
CFO, CIO and CEO: one sentence each and one ask, capacity for the people who use the most.

slides.notes: There are three things to do on Monday, and none of them needs anyone's permission. First, build the map: one page listing every system with an AI feature, who pays for its tokens, which model it uses, and what breaks when that model is down. Your CIO probably can't answer that last question today, and you can. Second, log your hours for two weeks: how long each day you keep a machine busy. Above five point three hours a day, owning the hardware pays for itself. The map and the hours are the two numbers that turn a conversation into a purchase order. Third, book three meetings, with the CFO, the CIO and the CEO, and bring one sentence for each and one ask: capacity for the people who use the most. The link on the last slide turns your answers into a one-page request.

slides.title: Intent is the new oil. Capping tokens is the leak.
slides.notes: The labs aren't the problem. The router still sends your hardest questions to the best models in the world, and it should. The problem is the default setup. By default, consumer plans can train on your data, deployments are metered, and companies cap their best people and then wonder why they leave. You're those people, so go get the capacity. Thank you. Let's take questions.
